emasculate.e: From Medieval Latin ēmasculātus, perfect passive participle of ēmasculō (“to emasculate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ē(x)- (“out, from, apart”) + masculus (“male, masculine”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), further from mās (“a man, a male”) + -culus (diminutive suffix).
emasculate.g: To deprive of virile or procreative power; to castrate, to geld.

emasculate.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ēmasculātus (more at Etymology 1), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).
emasculate.g: Deprived of virility or vigor; unmanned, weak.

embalm.e: From Middle English enbawmen, from Middle French embaumer, from Old French embasmer.
embalm.g: To treat a corpse with preservatives in order to prevent decomposition.

embarrassed.g: Having a feeling of shameful discomfort.

ember.e: From Middle English embre, eymbre, aymer, eymere, emeri, from Old English ǣmyrġe, from Proto-West Germanic *aimuʀjā, from Proto-Germanic *aimuzjǭ, a compound of *aimaz + *uzjǭ. The latter is from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ews- (“to burn”).
ember.g: A piece of coal or wood glowing by heat; a hot coal.

ember.e: From Middle English embryne (“running around, circuit”), from Old English ymbryne (“course; circuit”). Spelling changed through folk etymology. By surface analysis, umb- + run.
ember.g: Making a circuit of the year or the seasons; recurring in each quarter of the year, as certain religious days set apart for fasting and pray

embitter.e: From em- (variant of the suffix en- with the sense ‘to become’) + bitter.
embitter.g: To cause (something) to be or taste bitter; to bitter.

embolden.e: From bold (adjective) + em- -en (variant of en- -en (circumfix forming transitive verbs denoting an increase in, or intensification of, the quality denoted by the enclosed word)).
embolden.g: To render (someone) bolder or more courageous; to encourage, to hearten.

embrace.e: The English word is analysable as em- + brace.
embrace.g: To clasp (someone or each other) in the arms with affection; to take in the arms; to hug.

embroider.e: From Middle English embrouderen, frequentative of embrouden (“to decorate, embroider”), equivalent to embroid + -er. Middle English embrouden itself comes from Anglo-Norman embrouder, from Old French embrosder (“to embroider”), ultimately of Germanic origin, though the exact pathway is uncertain.
embroider.g: To stitch a decorative design on fabric with needle and thread of various colours.

emerald.e: From Middle English emeraude, borrowed from Old French esmeraude, from Vulgar Latin *smaralda, *smaraldus, *smaraudus, variant of Latin smaragdus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos), μάραγδος (máragdos), from a Semitic language.
emerald.g: Any of various green gemstones, especially a green transparent form of beryl, highly valued as a precious stone.

emerge.e: Borrowed from Middle French emerger, from Latin ēmergō (“to rise up or out”), from ē- (a variant of ex- (“out, forth”)) + mergō (“to dip, to sink”)

emerod.e: Variant of hemorrhoid; see there for more.
emerod.g: A haemorrhoid; an affliction mentioned in the Bible usually interpreted as a haemorrhoid.

eminent.e: From Middle French éminent, from Latin present participle ēminēns, ēminentis, from verb ēmineō (“to project, protrude”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + mineō, related to mons (English mount). Unrelated to emanate, which is instead from mānō (“to flow”).

emission.e: From Middle French émission, from Latin ēmissiō (“sending forth”), from ēmittō (“send out”), from ex (“from, out of”) + mittō (“send”).
emission.g: Something which is emitted or sent out; issue.

emphasize.e: Latin, from Ancient Greek – see emphasis. By surface analysis, emphasis + -ize.
emphasize.g: To stress, give emphasis or extra weight to (something).

empire.e: From Middle English empire, from Old French empire, empere, from Latin imperium, inperium (“command, control, dominion, sovereignty, a dominion, empire”), from imperare, inperare (“to command, order”), from in (“in, on”) + parare (“to make ready, order”).
empire.g: A political state, often a monarchy, that has achieved a much greater current size than its initial size by conquering surrounding territori

employ.e: From late Middle English emploien, imploien, emplien (“to apply to a specific purpose”), from Anglo-Norman emploier, Old French emploiier (“to entangle, fabricate, to make use of”), ultimately from Latin implicāre (“to infold, entangle, involve, engage”), from in- (“in”) + plicāre (“to fold”).
Borrowed from French emploi (“job, employment”), the deverbal from employer (“to put to use, to employ”), first attested in the late 17th century.
employ.g: The state of being an employee; employment.

employment.e: From employ (itself from Middle French employer, from Middle French empleier, from Latin implicō (“enfold, involve, be connected with”), itself from in- + plicō (“fold”)) + -ment.
employment.g: The occupation or work for which one is used, and often paid.

emptiness.e: From Middle English emptynesse, from Old English ǣmtiġnes. By surface analysis, empty + -ness.
emptiness.g: The state or feeling of being empty; an emotion that combines hollowness, numbness, disconnection and a lack of meaning in life, resulting i

empty.e: From Middle English emty, amty, from Old English ǣmtiġ, ǣmettiġ (“vacant, empty, free, idle, unmarried”, literally “without must or obligation, leisurely”), from Proto-Germanic *uz- (“out”) + Proto-Germanic *mōtijô, *mōtô (“must, obligation, need”), *mōtiþô (“ability, accommodation”), from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“measure.
empty.g: Devoid of content; containing nothing or nobody; vacant.

emulation.e: From Middle French émulation, from Latin aemulātiō.
emulation.g: The endeavor or desire to equal or excel someone else in qualities or actions.
